correctness.rationale: The basis-product constraints are equivalent to the original bilinear multiplicativity identity. The square equations propagate any zero column around the cycle. Otherwise the product of any two distinct columns is coordinatewise constant. A nonzero such product forces one column and then every other column to be everywhere nonzero; using two different other columns forces its inverse coordinates to have the same square. This uses n≥3 and injectivity, not surjectivity, of squaring. The square equations then force the constant-column images to agree. In the other branch all n supports are nonempty and disjoint in n positions, so each is a singleton. Comparing the square equation first at the support positions and then at their coefficients gives exactly rotations with unit coefficients. Both families preserve the defining products. The rank and count follow; composition of two line maps multiplies their scalars by n in the field. Multiplying an element of a nonzero ideal by one basis element and iterating gives every basis square; their span is the coordinate-sum hyperplane. The square-zero line is the constant line, which gives an algebra section precisely in odd dimension, and the monoid calculation gives exactly the listed idempotent retractions.
residual_risks: Finite replay is corroboration only. The proved result concerns field-valued maps, not the endomorphism scheme, other characteristics or n<3.

The parity switch has a concrete algebraic consequence, the existence of a complementary zero-product subalgebra to the square ideal.
